name: Tetrahydrocurcumin

lead: Tetrahydrocurcumin (THC) is a major metabolite of curcumin, the yellow compound in turmeric. Unlike curcumin it is colourless, which is why it appears in skin-brightening and anti-ageing products without staining skin.

The appearance angle is even skin tone and antioxidant support. Published work describes antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity mainly in lab and animal studies and in reviews of disease prevention.

paras: It is used as a cosmetic ingredient in topical products and as an oral supplement. Reviews note that curcumin's reduced metabolites, including THC, contribute to the biological activity attributed to curcumin.[2]

Wikipedia notes curcumin is a contact allergen and has poor bioavailability and a disputed research record.[1] Safety data on THC specifically are limited. People with turmeric allergies or on medication should consult a clinician.

angle.text: Products use it for brightening and antioxidant care; the cited research is mostly in other tissues and models.

lead: Tetrahydrocurcumin is a reduced metabolite of curcumin from turmeric (Curcuma longa).[1][2] It is of interest in cosmetics as a colourless curcuminoid for skin brightening and antioxidant care.

Reviews describe THC as preventing oxidative stress and inflammation and as having neuroprotective and anti-cancer activity in lab and animal models.[1] A review of curcumin's reductive metabolites says their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and other activities contribute to curcumin's effects, and identifies limitations that have hindered medical use.[2]

Wikipedia's curcumin article states that curcumin has poor bioavailability and that a US government program spent about $150 million on curcumin research from 1995 to 2017 without support for medical use.[3]

paras: THC is formed by reduction of curcumin, one of several reduced metabolites including di-, hexa- and octahydrocurcumin.[2]

Reviews cover chemoprevention, oxidative stress and inflammation,[1] and a 2025 randomized trial examined it in major depressive disorder.[4] A 2020 randomized study reported effects against hypoxia-induced cerebral oedema.[5]
No studies found on skin brightening. Human trials exist in other areas, such as a 2025 randomized trial in major depressive disorder.[4]
